mentions.quote: To Yama, residing in his hermitage, seated comfortably, a master of the Vedas and Śāstras
mentions.role: divine lawgiver and sage addressed by the sages, teacher of dharma

mentions.quote: tell that to us, O great sage
mentions.role: authority addressed for guidance on penance and purification

mentions.quote: Yama:
mentions.role: speaker delivering the laws of penance

entities.description: Yama is the deity of death and dharmic justice who acts as the authoritative lawgiver in this text, residing in a hermitage and instructing sages on penances.
entities.justification: Yama is named explicitly in the opening verse as the sage addressed by inquiring sages and is thereafter the primary speaker throughout chapter 1.

mentions.quote: the sages approached and asked, their minds held in check
mentions.role: questioners who approach Yama for instruction

mentions.quote:
The Sages:
Those who have committed great sins, and minor sinners as well, / by which vows they are purified—tell that to us, O great sage
mentions.role: inquirers requesting dharmic teaching

entities.description: An unnamed group of ascetic sages who approach Yama in his hermitage with disciplined minds to ask about purificatory penances for sinners.
entities.justification: The sages are explicitly named as the interlocutors in the framing verse (p-bb8187) and voice the opening question of the text.

mentions.quote: Having unknowingly eaten the food of an outcaste, or by chance the food of a Chandala
mentions.role: paradigmatic polluting group whose food causes impurity

mentions.quote: Chandalas and Mushtikas, and likewise those of mixed-caste birth
mentions.role: category of persons whose association requires penance

mentions.quote: Those who have intercourse with women of the Chandala and other such castes
mentions.role: group whose women's association requires severe penance

mentions.quote: both of these should be known as Chandalas, as should one born from a woman of the same gotra
mentions.role: social category assigned to those of polluted birth

mentions.quote: having him cast out by a Chandala
mentions.role: instrument of punishment and social degradation

entities.description: Chandalas are an outcast group occupying the lowest social position in the text's caste hierarchy, contact with whom generates severe ritual impurity requiring penance.
entities.justification: Chandalas appear across multiple verses as the paradigmatic polluting group and are used as a social marker for those of illegitimate birth.

mentions.quote: A twice-born who is touched by an impure substance, by night or by day, / should immediately bathe
mentions.role: subject of purification rules

mentions.quote: For cremating one killed by a cow or a Brahmin
mentions.role: figure whose death creates special pollution

mentions.quote: The four perpetrators of great sins
mentions.role: category whose great sins require horse-sacrifice-level penance

mentions.quote: A Brahmin who has abandoned his sacred fire, who has neglected his twilight prayers, / or who acts as a servant to a Shudra, the king should banish from the kingdom
mentions.role: subject of royal punishment for neglecting Brahminical duties

mentions.quote: A Brahmin who casts his seed in Shudra women, or who lusts after a Shudra woman, / the king should confiscate all his property
mentions.role: subject of penalty for caste transgression

entities.description: Brahmins are the highest-ranked varna in the text's social order, subject to the most stringent purity rules and the severest penalties when they transgress caste boundaries.
entities.justification: Brahmins are the most frequently referenced social group across both chapters as both the primary bearers of ritual purity obligations and the most severely penalized transgressors.

mentions.quote: taking up the skull-bowl is prescribed; / that Kāpālika vow is considered its ultimate penance by the wise
mentions.role: ascetic practice prescribed as ultimate penance for convergence of all sins

mentions.quote: For those who eat the food of a Kāpālika, and likewise for those who have intercourse with their women
mentions.role: polluting group whose food and women require year-long penance for association

entities.description: Kāpālikas are skull-bearing ascetics whose vow (carrying a skull-bowl) is prescribed as the ultimate penance for total convergence of sins, yet association with them also generates impurity.
entities.justification: The Kāpālika vow appears as the most extreme penance available in the text while Kāpālikas simultaneously function as a polluting group.

mentions.quote: who acts as a servant to a Shudra, the king should banish from the kingdom
mentions.role: social inferior whose service by a Brahmin is punishable

mentions.quote: A Brahmin who casts his seed in Shudra women
mentions.role: group whose women's association with Brahmins is heavily penalized

mentions.quote: A Shudra sitting on a high seat while a superior is present / shall be fined six paṇas
mentions.role: lowest varna subject to social deference rules

entities.description: Shudras occupy the lowest varna rank in the text and serve as the primary marker of caste pollution when associated with Brahmins, especially through sexual contact.
entities.justification: Shudras are recurrently invoked in both chapters as the defining boundary marker of varna transgression, particularly for Brahmin men.

mentions.quote: the killer among them, having been identified by divine ordeal, should be punished by those appointed by the king
mentions.role: executive authority who appoints punishment officers

mentions.quote: the king should have him killed with blows from a club
mentions.role: enforcer of violent punishment for harm to households

mentions.quote: the king should banish from the kingdom
mentions.role: authority who banishes delinquent Brahmins

mentions.quote: the king should confiscate all his property and brand his forehead with a vulva
mentions.role: punitive authority imposing bodily marking and confiscation

mentions.quote: Thus, the king should remove the five kinds of thorns from his kingdom; / his righteousness, wealth, lifespan, fame, and kingdom will increase
mentions.role: ideal ruler whose dharmic governance yields prosperity

entities.description: The king is the secular enforcement arm of dharma in the text, responsible for imposing fines, banishments, bodily punishments, and property confiscations for both ritual and civic offenses.
entities.justification: The king appears as the principal agent of legal punishment throughout both chapters, invoked dozens of times as the implementer of the text's legal rulings.

mentions.quote: the same for a Kuṇḍa or a Golaka (types of children born of adultery)
mentions.role: category of polluted birth requiring equivalent penance as a Sūta for killing

mentions.quote: A child born of adultery with a woman of the same caste is a Kuṇḍa if her husband is alive; / if the husband is dead, he is named a Golaka. Both are likewise devoid of caste status
mentions.role: adulterous offspring classified as casteless

mentions.quote: Children produced by twice-born men with the wives of other men, / whether of the same caste or not, are all known as Kuṇḍas and Golakas
mentions.role: illegitimate offspring denied both father's and mother's caste

entities.description: Kuṇḍas and Golakas are technical dharmaśāstra categories for children born of adultery who are denied caste status from either parent and are socially unmarriageable.
entities.justification: These terms are explicitly defined and categorized in consecutive verses of chapter 1 as juridical categories of illegitimate birth.

mentions.quote: Those who have committed great sins, and minor sinners as well, / by which vows they are purified—tell that to us, O great sage
these nine are apostates, excluded from all religious duties. / They are purified by a Cāndrāyaṇa, or by two Taptakṛcchras
When sinners wish to perform purifying penances like the Cāndrāyaṇa for their own good, / they should desire association with the good

themes.justification: The entire chapter 1 is structured as Yama's answer to the sages' question about purificatory vows, cataloguing specific penances (kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, Parāka, Taptakṛcchra) for specific sins.

mentions.quote: Having unknowingly eaten the food of an outcaste, or by chance the food of a Chandala, / one is purified in ten nights by a diet of barley gruel mixed with cow's urine
Those who are outside the four varṇas yet consider themselves Brahmins, / who are of mixed origin through generations, are to be carefully avoided
A Brahmin who serves a Shudra woman is considered lower than a Shudra

themes.justification: Violations of varna boundaries—especially Brahmin contact with Shudras and outcastes—constitute the largest single category of offense across both chapters, with graduated penalties by caste rank.

mentions.quote: for one who does not perform the vow in that case, the king should impose a fine of one thousand
Thus, the king should remove the five kinds of thorns from his kingdom; / his righteousness, wealth, lifespan, fame, and kingdom will increase
Of all thorns, the perpetrator of violence is the most powerful; / therefore, the king should devise a punishment of degradation for the violent

themes.justification: Chapter 2 explicitly articulates that penance is the religious remedy and royal fine is the civic enforcement mechanism, with the king's removal of 'thorns' producing his own dharmic flourishing.

themes.topic: Water and Twilight as Purifying Agents

mentions.quote: Touched by the wind and sun during the day, by the stars and breezes at night, / or by the two twilights, water is always purifying
In its natural state, not pervaded by any impure substance, it is always pure; / whether in a vessel or on the ground, drinkable water is a purifier of men
A twice-born who is touched by an impure substance, by night or by day, / should immediately bathe and touch fire; and at the two twilights, he is always pure

themes.justification: The text opens with a cosmological grounding of purity in natural elements—wind, sun, stars, twilight, and water—before proceeding to specific penances, establishing elemental purity as the foundation.

mentions.quote: A child born of adultery with a woman of the same caste is a Kuṇḍa if her husband is alive; / if the husband is dead, he is named a Golaka. Both are likewise devoid of caste status
One born from a fallen ascetic, and one born to a Brahmin woman from a Shudra man— / both of these should be known as Chandalas
They are not said to be of their mother's caste, nor are they considered to be of their father's caste; / such sons are unmarriageable

themes.justification: Multiple consecutive verses in chapter 1 construct a taxonomy of illegitimate births that disqualify offspring from both parental castes, showing the text's concern with the social pollution of irregular unions.

mentions.quote: The perpetrator, the consenter, the advisor, the instigator, the retaliator, / the planner, the helper, and the accomplice living with him are all to be killed
As long as one member of an undivided family performs a penance, / the others, by touching him, become impure and reprehensible
If a dependent, refugee, or servant commits a crime, he is the perpetrator; / the one who enjoys the fruit offered by him is not to be punished

themes.justification: The text elaborates a theory of distributed guilt in which proximity, benefit, and facilitation create degrees of culpability, distinguishing perpetrators, enablers, and innocent bystanders.

mentions.quote: To Yama, residing in his hermitage, seated comfortably, a master of the Vedas and Śāstras
this is sung by the Vedas and the sages who were consulted
this is understood by a wise Brahmin through the scriptures

themes.justification: The text grounds its authority implicitly in Yama's mastery of Vedas and Śāstras and explicitly invokes Vedic testimony as the ultimate validation of legal rulings, even in ambiguous cases.

mentions.quote: Ghee sold mixed with sesame oil under the name of ghee, / the merchant shall be made to pay four times the value
Pepper with stone fragments, salt with earth, / and asafoetida with tree resin—he shall likewise be made to pay four times the value
A superintendent of markets who uses false weights and measures, / shall be fined one paṇa

themes.justification: Chapter 2 contains a sustained passage on market fraud—adulteration of foodstuffs, false weights, and deceptive measures—showing the text's function as practical civil law beyond ritual prescription.
